question: Why Is Part of My Checkout Page Not Translating Correctly?
metaDescription: Custom or plugin-added checkout text often isn't wrapped in translation functions, or lacks a .po/.mo file entry — most translation plugins can't touch it.
shortAnswer: Standard WooCommerce checkout text is fully translatable through its own translation files, so a gap usually means the untranslated text is coming from somewhere else — a custom field added via code without proper translation functions, a third-party plugin's own text not included in the site's active translation, or a hardcoded string in a theme's checkout template override.

bodyHtml:
Why This Happens

WordPress and WooCommerce translations work through .po/.mo language files paired with translation function calls (__(), _e(), and similar) wrapping every translatable string in the code. Text that isn't wrapped in one of these functions, or that belongs to a plugin/theme without a translation file for the target language, simply can't be picked up by the site's active translation — it stays in whatever language it was originally written in, regardless of the site's language setting.

Common Causes

  • A custom checkout field added via code without wrapping its label or placeholder text in a translation function, which is a common oversight in quickly written custom snippets.
  • A third-party plugin (a specific gateway, a shipping method) that either doesn't support the target language at all, or has an incomplete translation missing specific strings.
  • A theme's checkout template override with hardcoded text baked directly into the template file, bypassing the translation system entirely.
  • An outdated translation file that hasn't been updated to include newer strings introduced in a more recent WooCommerce or plugin version.

How to Fix It

  1. Identify exactly which text isn't translating and where it's coming from (WooCommerce core, a specific plugin, or a theme template).
  2. For a plugin/theme without full translation support, a translation management plugin like Loco Translate can add custom translations even where the original source lacks them.
  3. For custom code, ensure all user-facing strings are properly wrapped in translation functions with a consistent text domain.
  4. Update outdated translation files after any plugin or WooCommerce version update that might have introduced new strings.

Need a multilingual checkout properly set up and tested? See custom WooCommerce development.
